To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of a room-temperature susceptometer to measure the liver iron concentration (LIC) of patients with iron overload is feasible and that LIC values measured by the susceptometer correlate with LIC values measured in biopsy specimens.

the use of the new, room-temperature susceptometry technique for assessing liver iron stores was highly accurate in patients with serum ferritin values of 1000 ng/mL or greater, but not in those with lower values, and that the technique was more accurate than the standard, room-temperature chemical method.
the use of a novel, low-cost, and noninvasive method for measuring hepatic iron content in patients with thalassemia and other forms of iron overload is feasible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new method for predicting hepatic iron overload in thalassemia major.
the development and application of new analytical techniques for the determination of the chemical composition and structure of the cell wall of bacteria.
the development and evaluation of a new, non-invasive, non-radioactive method of determining hepatic iron stores in patients with chronic liver disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of a combination of the three tests (serum ferritin, serum transferrin saturation, and hepatic iron concentration) provides the best diagnostic accuracy for the detection of hereditary hemochromatosis, and that the use of the three tests in combination is the best method for detecting hereditary hemochronatosis in the general population.
the use of iron chelation therapy is not recommended for patients with elevated ferritin levels who do not have evidence of iron overload by other means.
the use of the serum ferritin level to screen for iron overload is not recommended, but it can be used to identify patients who require further investigation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of room-temperature susceptometry to assess hepatic iron in individuals with elevated serum ferritisn (s-ferritin) is a useful and accurate method of predicting biopsy-determined hepical iron.
the use of the liver biopsy is not essential for the diagnosis and management of patients with elevated serum iron parameters.

we found that the room-temperature susceptometry (RTS) method was a good predictor of biopsy-determined hepical iron in patients with high serum ferritin levels and that the RTS method was a good method to follow the response to iron chelation therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there's no one size fits all for how to best manage iron levels.

there is a lot of variation between individuals in the relationship between iron stores and serum ferritin, and that this is a result of the fact that iron stores are not a simple linear function of serum ferritin, but rather are a nonlinear function.
we have shown that we can predict biopsy-determined hepical iron with a high degree of accuracy, even in patients with elevated ferritin.
